article.headline: WTO director warns fragmented regulations keep stablecoins to 3% of global payments
article.dek: Juan Marchetti says regulatory gaps limit stablecoin use despite their potential to ease trade‑finance friction, with only a fraction of jurisdictions having clear frameworks.
article.article_body:
At a Geneva briefing, Juan Marchetti, the World Trade Organization’s director of the trade‑in‑services and investment division, highlighted how divergent regulatory approaches are curbing stablecoin adoption in international finance. According to Marchetti, stablecoins could alleviate five major friction points in trade finance—high costs, low speed, limited access, insufficient transparency and foreign‑exchange constraints—but currently account for just 3 % of total cross‑border payments.

Marchetti attributed the low uptake to “regulation and the lack of development of regulatory frameworks,” emphasizing that only 39 % of the 28 jurisdictions surveyed in an October 2025 Financial Stability Board report have finalized stablecoin regulations. The WTO’s own study, launched alongside his speech, underscores that the fragmented regime hampers the technology’s potential, especially in developing economies that stand to benefit most from reduced remittance fees.

“Contribution to trade will depend far less on the technology than on regulatory convergence, interoperability and the surrounding financial infrastructure, especially in developing economies that stand to gain,” Marchetti said. He noted that while stablecoins have shown impressive growth—cross‑border stablecoin payments expanded 35‑fold between 2020 and mid‑2024—the lack of harmonized rules continues to restrict their share of global payments.

The WTO report also identified five friction points that stablecoins could improve, reinforcing the argument that policy alignment, rather than technological innovation, is the decisive factor for broader adoption. Major payment processors are already exploring stablecoin solutions; for instance, Mastercard recently partnered with the Borderless network to pilot a Crypto Credential framework aimed at increasing trust in cross‑border stablecoin transfers.

Marchetti’s remarks come as policymakers worldwide grapple with the challenge of crafting coherent regulatory standards that balance consumer protection, financial stability, and innovation. The WTO’s findings suggest that without coordinated regulatory action, stablecoins may remain a niche solution, despite their capacity to streamline trade finance and lower costs for emerging markets.
